paper_title: SWIFT: Self-guided Weak-to-strong dIFfusion models via Target extrapolation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Training high-quality diffusion models is computationally expensive, and inference-time guidance often adds further sampling cost. In this work, we introduce Swift, a simple yet effective self-guided training method that uses a frozen weak denoiser to improve a stronger model without adding inference overhead. For each noisy input, Swift extrapolates the clean regression target away from the weak denoiser's prediction, amplifying components that remain underfit. The weak guide can be an early training checkpoint, requires no backpropagation during main-model training, and is discarded afterward. The resulting model retains the original sampler and supports both conditional and unconditional generation without label dropout or an unconditional branch. We explain this mechanism through a spectral analysis of finite-time population gradient flow in an RKHS. With an early-stopped weak guide, we prove that a nonempty range of extrapolation strengths yields strictly lower posterior-mean error than matched standard training, despite shifting the regression target away from the posterior mean. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-256 demonstrate improvements across model scales and representations. In one ImageNet-256 configuration, Swift surpasses the baseline's best FID using roughly half the total training compute, including guide preparation and training overhead. On RAEv2, it achieves FID 1.15 without inference-time guidance and 0.99 with guidance. These results establish target extrapolation as an effective approach to weak-to-strong diffusion training with efficient single-model inference.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Diffusion models have achieved strong generative performance across images, video, and audio [8, 9, 12]. They are typically trained with simple denoising regression objective, yet many of the strongest generation results rely on guidance applied only at inference [7, 11]. In particular, autoguidance [11] shows that deliberately weaker denoiser can improve stronger one by defining an extrapolation direction during sampling. This suggests broader role for weak models: rather than serving as teachers to imitate, they can provide directions along which stronger predictor should move. Autoguidance realizes this idea by extrapolating the strong models prediction away from that of smaller or less-trained counterpart [11]. Related training-time approaches instead use evolving model predictions, intermediate supervision, or guidance-conditioned objectives [2, 28, 36, 39] (Section B). Can weak-to-strong extrapolation be moved from inference into training, so that the final denoiser itself benefits from the correction and the weak model can be discarded afterward? We introduce Swift, self-guided training method that uses frozen weak denoiser to construct extrapolated regression targets. For each noisy input, instead of regressing directly toward the clean sample, Swift moves the target farther in the direction from the weak prediction toward and beyond the clean sample. The weak denoiser therefore acts as directional reference, rather than teacher whose output should be imitated. It can be obtained from an early checkpoint of ordinary denoising training, remains fixed during the main training run, and requires no backpropagation. After training, the guide is discarded, leaving single denoiser and the original sampling procedure. The same construction applies to both conditional and unconditional generation. Our motivation is finite-time underfitting: because weak denoiser has learned less of the target function, extrapolating away from its prediction can amplify directions that remain underfit. We show theoretically that, for nonempty range of positive extrapolation strengths, deliberately shifting the training target in this way can produce predictor strictly closer to the original posterior mean than matched standard training (Theorem 1; proof in Section A.4). Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-256 show that the effect is not tied to particular representation or model family. On ImageNet-256, Swift improves diffusion models built on conventional VAE latents, representation-autoencoder latents [26, 38], end-to-end learned latent representations, and direct pixel-space generation. Across the evaluated DiffusionBench configurations [16], the same fixed Swift recipe lowers unguided FID in every configuration, and the improvement persists under longer training. The complete ImageNet comparisons and training trajectories are in Sections E.1 and E.4, and the additional CIFAR-10 experiments are in Section F. Swift also remains complementary to inference-time guidance. When guidance is independently retuned for the baseline and Swift, the Swift model achieves lower FID in every tested configuration (Table 7 and Section D.2). Moreover, on RAEv2 the preferred internal-guidance scale decreases from 1.78 for the baseline to 1.20 after Swift training, while the best guided gFID improves from 1.04 to 0.99 (Figure 4(b); Section E.3). This is consistent with Swift internalizing part of the weak-to-strong correction during training while leaving additional room for inference-time guidance. Our contributions are: Weak-to-strong learning through target extrapolation. We introduce Swift, which uses frozen weak denoiser as directional reference to extrapolate clean-sample regression targets. The guide is fixed during main-model training and discarded at inference (Section 2.2). Broad improvements across diffusion representations. We demonstrate consistent gains across CIFAR10 and ImageNet-256, spanning VAE, RAE, end-to-end latent, and pixel-space diffusion models. The gains persist under longer training and remain after inference-time guidance is independently retuned (Sections 5.1 and 5.2). finite-training explanation. We show theoretically that target extrapolation can strictly reduce posteriormean error relative to matched standard training over nonempty range of positive extrapolation strengths (Section 4).

sections.content: Building on the preliminaries, we introduce Swift, which trains denoiser using extrapolated regression targets. Instead of regressing directly onto the clean sample x0 as in Eq. (1), but using the extrapolated target: yα = x0 + α(cid:0)x0 Dweak(xt, σt)(cid:1) (5) Here, Dweak is pretrained, frozen weak denoiser, and α 0 sets the extrapolation strength. Setting α = 0 recovers standard denoising training. For α > 0, the target extends beyond the clean sample in the direction away from the weak denoisers prediction. Velocity-predicting models [18] apply the same extrapolation to the velocity, which is equivalent (Section D.1). Constructing the frozen weak denoiser. We train Dweak in the ordinary way with Eq. (1) and freeze it before the main run. The default guide uses smaller architecture; capacity and training-stage variants are studied separately. The default DiffusionBench guide has approximately one quarter as many parameters as the main denoiser and is trained for half the main models standard training duration; the CIFAR-10 and RAEv2 guide checkpoints are specified in Section D.1. The method is self-guided because the correction comes from weaker denoiser trained on the same task, without an external teacher, separate guidance objective, or an auxiliary prediction head. The intuition is to compensate for what ordinary training has not learned within finite training budget. Extrapolating the clean target away from Dweak emphasizes directions in which the weak denoisers prediction remains inaccurate. Whether this improves the main denoisers approximation to the posterior mean depends on how those directions relate to its own finite-training error. For frozen weak denoiser obtained by early stopping ordinary training, Section 4 and Theorem 1 establish conditions under which Swift achieves strictly lower posterior-mean error than baseline training (proofs in Section A; Gaussian-mixture illustration is in Section C). Training and inference. During training, only the main denoiser Dθ is optimized with Eq. (4). The weak denoiser Dweak is evaluated without gradients and remains fixed. Thus, for fixed clean sample, noise realization, and noise level, the regression target does not change as the main denoiser is updated. Beyond preparing the weak denoiser, each training step requires one additional weak-denoiser forward pass (about 9% more FLOPs on DiffusionBench; Section D.3). After training, it is discarded; sampling uses the trained denoiser and the original sampler, with no additional inference-time model evaluation (Section D.2).

sections.title: 3.2 Comparison with Training-Based Guidance
sections.content: MG constructs training correction using conditional and unconditional model predictions [28]. SGG studies incorporating guidance into training using an updated weak network or an intermediate prediction branch in its training-time variants [36]. GFT trains across guidance strengths using an unconditional prediction [2]. In these constructions, the auxiliary predictions can change as their models are trained. IG jointly supervises intermediate and final outputs for sampling-time guidance; it also studies training with detached final-minus-intermediate EMA correction [39, Sec. 6]. 5 These designs use changing prediction in the training correction or supervise an additional output. Swift obtains Dweak by ordinary denoising training and freezes it before training the main denoiser. For fixed training example and noise realization, its extrapolated target does not change as the main model is updated. This avoids joint optimization of the weak and main denoisers, which provided no clear additional endpoint benefit in our CIFAR-10 comparisons (Section F), and leaves single denoiser at inference. Preparing and evaluating the weak denoiser still incur training compute, which our compute comparisons account for (Section D.3). Further methodological details appear in Section and Eqs. (B.2) and (B.3).

sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate Swift on ImageNet-256 [3] and CIFAR-10 [13]. In every experiment Swift changes only the regression target; architectures, training schedules, samplers, and evaluation pipelines are kept the same as the baseline. On ImageNet, Swift uses one fixed recipe unless stated otherwise: α=0.4 with smaller pretrained guide frozen before main-model training. The default DiffusionBench guide is trained for half the main models standard training duration (Section D.1). Inspired by DiffusionBench [16], we evaluate Swift across 19 ImageNet-256 model Evaluation setup. configurations. For each configuration, we compare the baseline and Swift with and without inference-time guidance, tuning both guidance strengths separately where checkpoints are available and identifying published baselines otherwise. We report FID [6], sFID [21], precision and recall [14], representation-space FDr [32], and MIND [1] where available. Table 1 shows selected results; training and evaluation settings are in Sections D.1 and D.2, with complete ImageNet-256 and CIFAR-10 results in Sections and F.

Moderate positive α, half-width guide, and sufficiently trained weak guide give the strongest results. The CIFAR-10 training and evaluation settings are in Sections D.1 and D.2. Choosing α. Performance is broadly U-shaped in α (Figure 6(a)). On CIFAR-10, moderate positive values form broad favorable region around α = 0.70.9, where differences are comparable to replicate noise. ImageNet shows the same qualitative behavior: on DINOv2-B, α [0.5, 1.0] substantially improves over the baseline. The precise optimum depends on the model, however, so our breadth experiments use the fixed default α = 0.4 without tuning; in practice, small sweep over moderate positive values is sufficient. Negative α can accelerate the initial decrease in FID, but the tested negative warm starts provide no consistent final-quality advantage (Section F). Choosing the weak guide. The guide should be weaker than the student, but still competent. At α = 0.8 on CIFAR-10, reducing the channel base from the students 128 to 64 improves FID from 2.58 to 1.60, while substantially smaller guides degrade rapidly (Figure 6(b)). The half-width guide is also the best width across the tested α values on CIFAR-10 and consistently outperforms wider alternatives on ImageNet. Guide training length shows similar pattern: once the guide crosses competence threshold, performance is relatively insensitive over broad range (Figure 6(c)). On ImageNet, freezing the guide earlier can even help, with an earlier guide outperforming the default guide in our 50k re-evaluation; the corresponding training trajectories are discussed in Section E.4. simple fixed recipe gives substantial gains. The full CIFAR-10 campaign also tests jointly trained guides, capacity switches, and coefficients that change with training time or noise level (Section and Table 10). Co-training provides no clear additional endpoint benefit in the tested comparisons. Some early capacity switches and late coefficient profiles give useful CIFAR-10 refinements, whereas other schedules lose the gain; their effects depend on the guide and coefficient, and many small differences remain unresolved by repetitions. We therefore retain frozen half-width guide and fixed, moderate positive α as the simple default for the broader experiments.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: The regression target has received comparatively little attention as design choice in diffusion training, yet it turns out to be simple and effective place to intervene. By carrying the clean target past itself and away from frozen weak model, Swift moves weak-to-strong correction from inference into training, leaving single denoiser and the original sampler at deployment with only about 9% additional main-training FLOPs. Crucially, the modified target is not itself better estimator of the posterior mean: it is deliberately biased, yet finite training on it can produce better final predictor and better samples. This suggests broader view of the regression target as design interface rather than fixed quantityand raises the question of what other useful corrections can be written into it.

sections.title: Reproducibility statement
sections.content: Swift changes only the regression target: the objective is Eqs. (4) and (5), the frozen weak denoiser is constructed as described in Section 2.2, and everything else is the training loop of the respective framework. Section D.1 specifies guide architectures, freezing points, coefficients, training budgets, and hardware for the EDM, DiffusionBench, and RAEv2 models, and explains the velocity-target implementation. Section D.2 specifies samplers, guidance and checkpoint selection, and evaluation metrics, distinguishing re-evaluated pairs from published baselines; Section D.3 reports the GPU hours and the FLOPs accounting behind Figures 1 and 5. Section gives all 19 ImageNet-256 configurations with and without guidance on all 15 metrics, and Section the CIFAR-10 experiments, including an account of all 156 launched (152 scored) arms (Section F). The matched Gaussian-mixture comparison is specified in Section C, and all assumptions and proofs are in Section A. Our implementation will be made publicly available upon publication.

sections.title: D Experimental Setup
sections.content: We specify training (Section D.1), evaluation (Section D.2), and compute accounting (Section D.3). In matched comparisons, Swift changes only the training target, leaving the models architecture, optimizer, schedule, sampler, and evaluator fixed. In the default frozen-guide recipe, the guide receives the same noisy image (or latent), noise level, and class condition as the main denoiser. Its prediction is evaluated without gradients and used only to construct the target in Eq. (5); the original noise distribution, loss weighting, and optimizer update are retained. The frozen guide is not an inference-time component. D.1 Training Configurations CIFAR-10. We use the EDM configuration of Karras et al. [10]: class-conditional DDPM++ model at 32 32 resolution with EDM preconditioning and loss weighting, batch size 512, fp32 training, and 200,000-kimg horizon (kimg = 103 training images). The main denoiser uses channel base 128 (cb128). Guide capacity is specified by channel base (cb16cb128), with cb64 denoting the default half-width guide. NCSN++ and ADM-style guide variants use the corresponding channel bases; their full results are reported in Section F. The default guide is separately trained, class-conditional DDPM++ cb64 model frozen at 200,000 kimg. Unless sweep changes it, α is fixed scalar. The α = 0 arm (D0) is the ordinary-training reference at the same main-model budget and evaluation endpoint; it is not new seed-matched baseline trained for every exploratory setting. Section and the accompanying DATA/ ledger distinguish repeated runs, guide variants, and incomplete or extended runs. ImageNet-256, DiffusionBench. Our main DiffusionBench model [16] uses representation-autoencoder tokenizer [38] over frozen DINOv2-B features [22] and 615M-parameter decoupled diffusion transformer [30]. 25 The breadth study keeps the 615M-parameter training recipe while varying the tokenizer or using pixel-space model (Section E.1). The model is trained class-conditionally with global batch size 1024 for 80 epochs, corresponding to 1251 optimizer steps per epoch, and is evaluated every five epochs. Unless stated otherwise, the 18 DiffusionBench configurations use the same Swift recipe: α = 0.4 and separate guide for the corresponding model, pretrained for half the main models standard training duration and then frozen. Each half-width guide has about 155M parameters and approximately one quarter of the main denoisers forward-pass FLOPs. The short-guide ablation freezes the same architecture at an earlier checkpoint. CFG is used only at sampling time and is tuned independently for the baseline and Swift. The ImageNet backends use linear flow matching, xt = (1 t)x0 + tϵ and = ϵ x0, with ϵ (0, I), rather than the additive-noise parameterization of Section 2.1. Most DiffusionBench configurations predict velocity. At fixed noisy input and time, velocity is affine in the clean prediction. The implementation constructs the main loss target in velocity space: vSwift = (1 + α)v αvg, This is equivalent to extrapolating the clean-sample target and then converting it to velocity (apart from numerical clamping near time endpoint). For clean-sample-prediction configurations, including RAEv2, the bxg is first converted to vg = (xt bxg)/ max(t, ε); the model likewise converts the main output guide output before computing its velocity-space loss. The guide is detached, and RAEv2s internal-guidance auxiliary head retains its ordinary target. The main DiffusionBench sweep is trained on 4B200 GPUs. Longer-training experiments use the same optimization configuration and are run on 8H100 GPUs where noted. ImageNet-256, RAEv2. We use the released 875M-parameter, class-conditional DINOv3-L configuration of Singh et al. [26] (dinov3l-k7) together with its native internal-guidance implementation. The k7 encoder sums layers 11, 13, 15, 17, 19, 21, 23. The main model predicts clean latents and trains for up to 160 epochs (global batch 1024, bf16, 8B200 GPUs). The matched baseline keeps the models gMuon schedule (learning rate 2 104, 25-epoch warmup, decay to 2 105 by epoch 50), latent preprocessing, and EMA decay 0.9995. The Swift guide is the models GUIDE-w05 weak-model configuration, loaded from pretrained checkpoint and frozen before main-model training. Unless stated otherwise, we use α = 0.4. The guide components use (width, depth, heads) = (720, 28, 10) and (1024, 2, 8); w05 denotes approximately half the models parameters, not half of every hidden width. All other architectural and optimization settings follow the released RAEv2 configuration. D.2 Sampling and Evaluation Settings Table 5 summarizes our evaluation settings.
